Today we’re releasing Muse Spark Open, the most capable US open-weight model to date.

Built for coding and agentic work, it excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning.

Key Model Specs:
→ 816B total / 42B active parameters
→ 1M token context window
→ Natively multimodal across text, image, video, audio

Given plain-language instructions, Claude Mythos 5 designed quantum circuits that improve on the best published ones, sometimes by an order of magnitude or more.

More efficient circuits reduce the resources needed by quantum algorithms, which could bring quantum computing applications in chemistry and materials science within reach sooner.

posts.text:
HOLY SHIT.

For crypto, this is one of the most insane posts of the year, but I'm guessing most people don't understand it.

Let me explain...

Bitcoin's accounts, and subsequently Ethereum's (and therefore every other EVM chain's), are built on a specific elliptic curve called secp256k1.

secp256k1 is a different elliptic curve from the one used across nearly every modern hardware device, including iPhones.

Modern devices mostly use a different curve called secp256r1, which is usually referred to as P-256 - one of the curves investigated in the article.

This mismatch has made it sooo difficult in the past to integrate crypto accounts natively into the security systems of modern hardware.

For example, Apple's Secure Enclave natively supports P-256, not secp256k1.

This has prevented crypto accounts from being able to use the same hardware protection as things like Apple Pay.

Same goes for the web with passkeys - WebAuthn uses P-256 signatures, which means Ethereum accounts using secp256k1 can't use them natively either.

But why did Satoshi do this?

The main theory for choosing secp256k1 was distrust of the P-256 curve - i.e. he thought there was an NSA backdoor.

A "backdoor" here basically means a secret, intentional weakness in the curve that would allow the NSA to exploit it and access private keys.

This was because P-256 was created with involvement from the NSA...

And the NSA provided a mysterious "seed" used to generate one of the curve's parameters without explaining where that seed came from.

This eventually transformed into a ~25-year-old mystery with a 5-figure reward for finding where this seed came from.

Claude figured it out in less than 30 mins. 

And the best part is its internal thinking was: "Hmm wait... is it suspicious that such an obvious thing wasn’t discovered in 25 years?"

The solution was stupidly simple - just the time the curve was created, put into a specific random number generator function.

This doesn't 100% prove there's no backdoor yet, but it provides strong evidence that this seed wasn't secretly engineered by the NSA.

And Claude did this with "just a simple prompt" in under 30 minutes.
posts.why_viral: Clear, technical explanation of why Claude solving the NIST curve seed mystery matters for crypto hardware and security.
posts.why_it_matters: Turns a research announcement into practical context for anyone building or securing blockchain systems.

posts.text:
Why are you still using pull requests?

Is it for code review?

If so, do you really think your or your colleagues catch bugs and mistakes that an Opus 5.5 or Fable or Astra won't find? You can literally spawn all three of them and have them check four times each.

(Also, don't tell me you don't have a "stamp plz" Slack channel or group chat somewhere.)

Is it for knowledge sharing?

Surely there's better ways for that now than the PR, no? We have models that can generate explainer videos, presentations, podcasts, games, quizzes, walkthroughs, ... for any piece of code it can reach. 

Is CI the reason?

Well ackshually, CI means continuous integration and its original meaning is the *opposite* of having long-lived branches and PRs.

But, leaving that aside, your agents are hopefully already running the tests before they push something, and hopefully they can run as long as they want and don't block you so they can run the whole test suite and generate "irrefutable proof" and end-to-end demo videos and so on... And so they run the tests and confirm and then you push to a branch and everything runs again and then you merge and then it runs again? That doesn't make sense, does it?

Maybe you work in open source and you accept contributions, in which case I can't speak to the value of pull requests. It's been 2 years since my last OSS contribution. But from what I heard, the time of the PR is coming to an end in OSS too?

I honestly don't get why people still stick to PRs.

With agents you can now move 10x faster, you can finally do real continuous integration, and get more confidence in the changes the agent made.

Don't slow yourself down by having all the changes pile up in a PR.
posts.why_viral: Sharp, practical argument that traditional PRs are obsolete once agents can review, test, and explain code.
posts.why_it_matters: Challenges default engineering process assumptions for teams shipping with coding agents.
